title: Create quality-summary.sh deterministic script
description:
Create a scripts/quality-summary.sh that runs all quality checks and outputs a structured JSON summary. Currently, both the implementation subagent and code reviewer run terminal commands (task lint, task test:unit, etc.) and must interpret pages of raw terminal output to determine pass/fail status. This wastes context tokens and introduces interpretation errors.

## Why this matters

This is the 'deterministic offloading' pattern — one of the most impactful optimizations in agent systems. The idea: anything that can be computed deterministically should NOT be done by the LLM. Instead, wrap it in a script that returns structured data the LLM can consume in one read.

Real-world impact:
- Raw pytest output: ~200-500 lines → ~2000-5000 tokens of context
- Raw ruff output: ~50-200 lines
- Raw mypy output: ~30-100 lines
- Structured JSON summary: ~20 lines → ~200 tokens

That's a 10-25x reduction in context window usage for quality checks alone. And it's deterministic — no LLM interpretation needed, no risk of misreading a passing test as failing.

This pattern is recommended by Anthropic ('use tools to compute, not the model'), LangChain ('deterministic tool outputs'), and is standard in CI/CD systems (structured test reporters like JUnit XML).

## What to create

scripts/quality-summary.sh that:
1. Runs task lint (ruff check + format)
2. Runs task typecheck (mypy)
3. Runs task test:unit (pytest)
4. Captures exit codes and key metrics
5. Outputs a single JSON object to stdout

Example output:
{
  "lint": {"passed": true, "errors": 0, "warnings": 2},
  "typecheck": {"passed": true, "errors": 0},
  "tests": {"passed": true, "total": 142, "passed_count": 142, "failed_count": 0, "skipped": 3},
  "overall": "PASS"
}

## What to change

- Add a task quality:summary to Taskfile.yml that wraps this script
- Reference in implementation-subagent and code-review-subagent

## User feedback points

- Review the JSON output format
- Decide which checks to include (lint + typecheck + tests, or also coverage + complexity?)
- Decide whether to add this as a Taskfile task or keep as standalone script
- Review whether the script should fail-fast or always run all checks
acceptance_criteria:
- scripts/quality-summary.sh created and executable
- Outputs valid JSON to stdout
- Covers lint, typecheck, and test results
- Exit code reflects overall pass/fail
- Taskfile task added (task quality:summary)
- Script tested and working

title: Extract style guides to orchestrator-templates skill
description:
Move the three inline style guides from the orchestrator prompt into a loadable skill file. The orchestrator currently carries ~800 tokens of static template text (phase_complete_style_guide, plan_complete_style_guide, git_commit_style_guide) on every single invocation, even when it's just doing research or waiting for user input.

## Why this matters

This is a classic context window optimization. LLM context windows are finite and expensive. Every token of 'always-loaded' content competes with the actual task content (code, file listings, user messages). The community calls this 'prompt bloat' — static reference material that's rarely needed but always present.

The skill-loading pattern is the recommended approach:
- GitHub Copilot agents support @-referencing skill files on demand
- Claude Code skills use the same pattern — load SKILL.md only when needed
- This mirrors the 'lazy loading' pattern in software: don't load what you don't need yet

Impact: The orchestrator only needs style guides at Phase 2C (writing completion files) and Phase 3 (writing plan completion). That's maybe 10% of its lifetime. The other 90% of the time, those 800 tokens are dead weight.

## What to create

.github/skills/orchestrator-templates/SKILL.md containing:
- Phase completion file template
- Plan completion file template
- Git commit message style guide
- Usage instructions for when to load

## What to change

orchestrator.agent.md:
- Remove inline style guides
- Add instruction: 'When writing completion files, load the orchestrator-templates skill'
- This should reduce the orchestrator prompt by ~35-40%

## User feedback points

- Review the extracted skill file content
- Decide whether the Claude Code mirror (.claude/skills/) should also be created
- Approve the reduced orchestrator prompt
acceptance_criteria:
- Skill file created at .github/skills/orchestrator-templates/SKILL.md
- All three style guides moved out of orchestrator prompt
- Orchestrator references skill for on-demand loading
- Orchestrator prompt reduced by ~35-40%
- Templates are identical to originals (no content loss)

title: Create implementation subagent
description:
Create a lightweight, dedicated implementation-subagent.agent.md file (~15 lines). This follows the hybrid approach: scoped tools and output contract in the agent file, but task-specific instructions come from the orchestrator at invocation time.

## Why lightweight over heavy

A heavy agent (50+ lines) constrains the orchestrator's ability to tailor instructions per task — e.g., 'this involves Rust FFI, focus on memory safety' or 'docs-only change, skip tests'. A lightweight agent provides structural guardrails (tool scoping, output contract, direct-invocation guard) while the orchestrator retains full flexibility to adapt instructions contextually.

This is the hybrid pattern recommended by Anthropic's 'Building Effective Agents' guide: use explicit agent definitions only for structural concerns (tools, trust boundary, output format), not for behavioral micromanagement.

## What to create

.github/agents/implementation-subagent.agent.md (~15 lines) containing:
- Frontmatter: tool set scoped to edit, search, read, execute/runInTerminal, execute/getTerminalOutput, execute/createAndRunTask, execute/testFailure, todo
- Explicit exclusions via frontmatter: no web, no agent (no sub-subagents)
- Output format: JSON referencing implementation-output.schema.json
- Default quality check instruction: run task lint and task test:unit before returning
- Direct-invocation guard (redirect users to orchestrator)
- One-line delegation: 'Follow the orchestrator task-specific instructions'

The orchestrator retains full freedom to add per-task context in its invocation message.

## User feedback points

- Approve the tool set (should implementation subagent have web access for docs lookups?)
- Review the ~15-line agent file
- Decide if quality checks should be 'must run' or 'run unless orchestrator says otherwise'
acceptance_criteria:
- implementation-subagent.agent.md exists in .github/agents/
- Tool set follows principle of least privilege
- Output contract references JSON schema
- Direct-invocation guard included
- Quality gate requirements documented

title: Design JSON schemas for inter-agent communication
description:
Create JSON schema files that define the contract between the orchestrator and each subagent. These schemas formalize what each subagent must return, replacing the current free-form markdown approach.

## Why this matters

In multi-agent systems, the handoff between agents is the weakest link. Anthropic's 'Building Effective Agents' guide and OpenAI's multi-agent documentation both identify unstructured inter-agent communication as the #1 cause of cascading failures. When Agent A returns prose instead of structured data, Agent B must use natural language understanding to parse it — introducing non-determinism, potential data loss, and wasted context tokens on parsing instructions.

JSON schemas give us:
1. **Validation contract** — the orchestrator knows exactly what fields to expect
2. **Self-documentation** — new contributors understand the interface by reading the schema
3. **Machine-parseability** — the orchestrator can detect missing/malformed fields and retry
4. **Token efficiency** — structured output is more compact than prose

## What to create

Three schema files in .github/agents/schemas/:
- research-output.schema.json — researcher subagent output contract
- review-output.schema.json — code review subagent output contract
- implementation-output.schema.json — implementation subagent output contract

## User feedback points

- Review each schema before it's finalized
- Decide on additional fields (e.g., confidence score for researcher, quality_checks for reviewer)
- Approve the schema directory location (.github/agents/schemas/ vs alternatives)

## Learning context

JSON Schema (json-schema.org) is the de-facto standard for describing JSON structures. It's used by OpenAPI, VS Code settings, GitHub Actions, and most LLM structured-output APIs. The schemas here aren't enforced programmatically (LLMs don't validate against schemas at runtime) but serve as a prompt-engineering contract that dramatically improves output consistency.
acceptance_criteria:
- Three JSON schema files created in .github/agents/schemas/
- Each schema has required/optional fields documented
- Schemas reviewed and approved by user
- Schemas are valid JSON Schema draft-07

title: Epic: Optimize agent orchestration system
description:
Overhaul the 3-agent orchestration system (.github/agents/) to improve determinism, reduce context window waste, and enforce structured communication between orchestrator and subagents.

## Motivation

The current agent system (orchestrator + researcher + code-review subagents) works but has several inefficiencies identified through a best-practices audit:
- Subagent outputs are free-form markdown — non-deterministic, hard to parse
- The orchestrator carries ~800 tokens of static style guides inline
- Subagents can be invoked directly by users without proper context
- No dedicated implementation subagent exists (uses default agent)
- Tools are over-provisioned on subagents (principle of least privilege violated)
- No explicit retry policy for failed subagent invocations

## Scope

7 tasks covering: JSON schemas for inter-agent communication, new implementation subagent, style guide extraction to skills, quality-summary script, subagent refactoring, orchestrator refactoring.

## Success Criteria

- All subagent outputs follow JSON schemas
- Orchestrator prompt reduced by ~40%
- Subagents refuse direct user invocation
- Quality checks are deterministic via script
- Implementation subagent has explicit definition

2. **Error handling consistency** — do all adapters, runners, and lifecycle hooks follow the error handling patterns from ADR-011?
3. **Test coverage gaps** — are there modules with low or no coverage? Are edge cases adequately tested?
4. **Dependency hygiene** — are all dependencies necessary and pinned appropriately? Any unused or redundant deps?
5. **Documentation completeness** — do all public APIs have docstrings? Are the guides current with the actual implementation?

8. **Performance considerations** — any obvious bottlenecks in the MQTT publish path, filter pipeline, or persistence layer?
9. **ADR compliance** — are all accepted ADRs actually implemented? Any drift?

A review document with categorized findings, plus beads tasks for anything that should be addressed before 0.3.0.

title: Evaluate project folder restructuring (src + tests)
description:
Evaluate whether the flat module layout in packages/src/cosalette/ (39 files) and packages/tests/unit/ (43 files) should be restructured into sub-packages for clarity and maintainability before 0.3.0.

## Current state

- packages/src/cosalette/ has 39 files in a single flat directory — no sub-packages
- packages/tests/unit/ has 43 test files, all at the same level
- Navigation and discoverability suffer as the module count grows
- Logical groupings exist but aren't expressed in the directory tree

## Potential groupings to evaluate

Source (packages/src/cosalette/):
- core/ — _app, _context, _wiring, _injection, _registration, _runner_utils, _clock
- mqtt/ — _mqtt, _mqtt_client, _router
- devices/ — _telemetry_runner, _command, _command_runner, _strategies
- health/ — _health, _errors, _retry
- persistence/ — _persist, _stores
- filters/ — _filters, filters, _filters_rs.*
- config/ — _settings, _cli, _logging
- util/ — _utils, _json, _introspect, _version

Tests (packages/tests/unit/):
- Mirror src sub-package structure

## Evaluation criteria

1. Does restructuring improve discoverability for new contributors?
2. What is the migration cost (import path changes, downstream apps)?
3. Does it conflict with any ADRs (especially ADR-006 hexagonal architecture)?
4. How does it affect the public API surface (__init__.py re-exports)?

An ADR (accept or reject) with the chosen structure or justification for keeping flat.

title: Release-gated GitHub Pages deploy (modify release-please.yml)
description:
Add documentation build and GitHub Pages deployment to the release-please workflow, so official docs only update on actual releases.

## Current Behavior

- release-please.yml handles version bumps, wheel builds, SBOM, and PyPI publishing
- GitHub Pages deploy happens on every push to main (in docs.yml)

## Target Behavior

- GitHub Pages deploy ONLY happens when release_created == true
- Docs are built from the release tag (not main HEAD)
- Deployed via actions/upload-pages-artifact + actions/deploy-pages (same mechanism as before)

## Implementation

Add a new job to release-please.yml:

```yaml
deploy-docs:
  name: Deploy Documentation to GitHub Pages
  needs: release-please
  if: needs.release-please.outputs.release_created == 'true'
  runs-on: ubuntu-latest
  permissions:
    pages: write
    id-token: write
    contents: read
    packages: read
  environment:
    name: github-pages
    url: ${{ steps.deployment.outputs.page_url }}
  steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v6
      with:
        ref: ${{ needs.release-please.outputs.tag_name }}
    - # Build docs inside devcontainer
    - # Validate build output
    - uses: actions/upload-pages-artifact@v4
      with: { path: site }
    - uses: actions/configure-pages@v5
    - uses: actions/deploy-pages@v4
      id: deployment
```

## Permission Note

The release-please.yml currently has contents: write and pull-requests: write at the job level. The new deploy-docs job needs pages: write and id-token: write — these should be scoped to that job only.

## Acceptance Criteria

- GitHub Pages is only updated when a release is created
- Docs are built from the release tag
- Official docs URL (ff-fab.github.io/cosalette/) always matches the latest release
- Existing release-please jobs are not affected

title: PR documentation preview workflow (docs-preview.yml)
description:
Create .github/workflows/docs-preview.yml adapted from cosalette-apps.

## Implementation

Simplified version of cosalette-apps' docs-preview.yml (no monorepo merging needed):

### Triggers
- pull_request (opened/synchronize/reopened) → build + deploy jobs
- pull_request_target (closed) → teardown job

### Path filters
docs/**, zensical.toml, uv.lock

### Jobs

**build** (if action != closed):
1. Checkout code
2. Build docs inside devcontainer (task docs:build)
3. Validate site/index.html exists
4. Upload site/ as artifact (docs-preview, retention 3 days)

**deploy** (needs build, if action != closed):
1. Download docs-preview artifact
2. npm install -g surge && surge site/ cosalette-pr-{N}.surge.sh
3. Build changed-pages links from PR diff (simplified: only docs/*.md → /<slug>/)
4. Post/update PR comment with preview URL + changed page links using peter-evans actions

**teardown** (if action == closed, uses pull_request_target):
1. surge teardown cosalette-pr-{N}.surge.sh
2. Update PR comment with strikethrough URL

### Environment
- DEVCONTAINER_IMAGE: ghcr.io/ff-fab/cosalette-devcontainer
- SURGE_DOMAIN: cosalette-pr-${{ github.event.pull_request.number }}.surge.sh
- Secrets: SURGE_TOKEN

### Permissions
contents: read, packages: read, pull-requests: write

### Concurrency
group: docs-preview-${{ github.event.pull_request.number }}, cancel-in-progress: true

## Reference
- cosalette-apps/.github/workflows/docs-preview.yml

## Acceptance Criteria
- Workflow runs on PRs that change docs
- Preview deployed to surge.sh with deterministic per-PR domain
- PR comment posted with preview URL and changed-page links
- Preview torn down when PR is closed
- Graceful skip if SURGE_TOKEN not set (fork PRs)

title: ADR-030: Documentation Hosting Strategy
description:
Write ADR documenting the three-tier documentation hosting strategy decision.

## Decision

- PR previews deployed to surge.sh (cosalette-pr-{N}.surge.sh)
- Main branch docs deployed to surge.sh (cosalette-main.surge.sh)  
- Official docs deployed to GitHub Pages only on release-please releases
- GitHub Pages always reflects the latest published release

## Context

- cosalette releases are less frequent than main branch updates
- Users following official docs may encounter unreleased features
- PR authors need preview capability for documentation changes
- cosalette-apps already uses surge.sh for PR previews (reference implementation)

## Acceptance Criteria

- Documents the three-tier approach, alternatives considered, and rationale

title: Epic: Documentation Hosting Strategy
description:
Implement a three-tier documentation hosting strategy using surge.sh and release-gated GitHub Pages deployment.

## Problem

cosalette's documentation on GitHub Pages always reflects main, which runs ahead of releases. Users reading the official docs may see features that haven't been released yet. PR authors can't preview documentation changes before merging.

## Solution

Three-tier documentation hosting:

| Tier            | Host         | URL                              | Updated When              |
|-----------------|--------------|----------------------------------|---------------------------|
| PR Preview      | surge.sh     | cosalette-pr-{N}.surge.sh       | Every PR push (torn down on close) |
| Main (dev)      | surge.sh     | cosalette-main.surge.sh         | Every push to main        |
| Official (rel)  | GitHub Pages | ff-fab.github.io/cosalette/     | Only on release-please releases |

## Reference Implementation

cosalette-apps (https://github.com/ff-fab/cosalette-apps) has a docs-preview.yml workflow for PR previews on surge.sh. This epic adapts and extends that pattern.

## Prerequisites

- SURGE_TOKEN repository secret must be configured
- peter-evans/find-comment@v3 and peter-evans/create-or-update-comment@v4 actions for PR comments

description:

5. Dict value type conflicts with adapter port type → ValueError at registration

16. Per-device config available alongside app-wide Settings and adapters

19. publish= shared across all dict-registered devices

title: Design and implement dict-based multi-device decorator with per-device config injection
description:
Extend @app.telemetry (and @app.device, @app.command) to accept a callable returning
a dict[str, T] for the name parameter, enabling settings-driven multi-device
registration with automatic per-device config injection — all from a single decorator.

This is an additive convenience on TOP of @app.on_configure (not a replacement).
@app.on_configure remains the general-purpose solution for heterogeneous devices.
The dict-name decorator is a shorthand for the common homogeneous case.

## Motivation

After @app.on_configure (COS-3cg.2) solves the eager-settings crash, apps still need a
factory function (make_calendar_handler, make_cover) to create per-device closures that
capture config. For telemetry-only cases this is boilerplate — the handler is identical
across devices, only the config differs.

## Proposed API

### Core pattern: name= as callable returning dict

```python
@app.telemetry(
    name=lambda s: {sensor.name: sensor for sensor in s.sensors},
    interval=1500,
    retry=3,
    retry_on=(BleConnectionError,),
)
async def _telemetry(
    config: SensorConfig,   # ← auto-injected per device from dict value
    reader: AirthingsReaderPort,
) -> dict[str, object]:
    reading = await reader.read(config.mac)
    return {"temperature": reading.temperature}
```

The framework:
1. Resolves the callable after settings are available (same as deferred intervals)
2. Gets back {"sensor_a": SensorConfig(...), "sensor_b": SensorConfig(...)}
3. Registers one telemetry device per key, each with the dict value registered in
   per-device DI scope by its type — type(value) is the DI key
4. Handler parameters resolved via DI: SensorConfig matches the per-device value

### name= parameter type expansion

Current:  name: str | None
Proposed: name: str | None | NameSpec

where:
```python
type NameSpec = Callable[[Settings], list[str] | dict[str, Any]]
```

- list[str] → register N devices with identical handler, no per-device config
  (handler can use ctx.name to disambiguate if needed)
- dict[str, T] → register N devices, each with T injected via DI

### Per-device interval (optional, can defer to v2)

When name returns a dict, interval can optionally also be per-device:

```python
@app.telemetry(
    name=lambda s: {cal.key: cal for cal in s.calendars},
    interval=lambda config: config.poll_interval,  # receives per-device config
)
async def calendar(config: CalendarConfig, reader: CalDavPort) -> dict[str, object]:
    events = await reader.read_events(url=config.url, ...)
    return {"events": [...]}
```

How this works:
- If name returns dict[str, T] AND interval is Callable with parameter annotated
  as T (not Settings), the framework calls interval(value) per device
- If interval is Callable[[Settings], float] (existing), it's called once (shared)
- If interval is float, it's shared across all devices

This enables caldates2mqtt to have per-calendar poll intervals from a single decorator.

Implementation approach for per-device interval:
- Inspect the interval callable's type annotations
- If the first param matches the dict value type → per-device resolution
- If the first param is Settings (or subclass) → existing shared resolution
- This is resolved during the registration phase, not at module import time

### How it works for each app

**airthings2mqtt — multi-sensor (currently single device):**
Before:
```python
# Would need @app.on_configure + loop + make_handler factory
@app.on_configure
def register(settings: Airthings2MqttSettings) -> None:
    for sensor in settings.sensors:
        app.add_telemetry(sensor.name, make_sensor_handler(sensor), interval=...)
```

After (dict pattern):
```python
@app.telemetry(
    name=lambda s: {sensor.name: sensor for sensor in s.sensors},
    interval=lambda s: s.poll_interval,
    retry=3,
    retry_on=(BleConnectionError, BleTimeoutError),
)
async def _telemetry(
    config: SensorConfig,
    reader: AirthingsReaderPort,
) -> dict[str, object]:
    reading = await reader.read(config.mac)
    return {"temperature": reading.temperature, ...}
```

**caldates2mqtt — multi-calendar with per-device interval:**
Before (with on_configure):
```python
@app.on_configure
def register(settings: CalDates2MqttSettings) -> None:
    for cal in settings.calendars:
        app.add_device(cal.key, make_calendar_handler(cal))
```

After (dict pattern on @app.device):
```python
@app.device(
    name=lambda s: {cal.key: cal for cal in s.calendars},
)
async def calendar_device(
    ctx: DeviceContext,
    cal: CalendarConfig,   # ← per-device config injected
    reader: CalDavPort,
    logger: logging.Logger,
) -> None:
    @ctx.on_command
    async def _handle_command(topic: str, payload: str) -> None:
        await _read_and_publish(ctx, reader, cal)

    while not ctx.shutdown_requested:
        await _read_and_publish(ctx, reader, cal)
        await ctx.sleep(cal.poll_interval)
```

This eliminates the make_calendar_handler factory entirely! The closure is replaced
by DI — CalendarConfig is injected per device from the dict value.

**velux2mqtt — multi-cover (complex @app.device):**
```python
@app.device(
    name=lambda s: {cover.name: cover for cover in s.covers},
)
async def cover_device(
    ctx: DeviceContext,
    cover_cfg: CoverConfig,       # ← per-device from dict
    settings: Velux2MqttSettings,  # ← app-wide from DI
) -> None:
    gpio = ctx.adapter(GpioSwitchPort)
    tracker = PositionTracker(
        travel_duration_up=cover_cfg.travel_duration_up, ...
    )
    # ... rest of handler creates per-device state as local variables
```

Even for velux2mqtt's complex case, the factory pattern is eliminated.

## Interaction with existing features

- **init= callback**: When name is a dict, the dict value acts as an implicit init.
  Using both dict-name and init= is allowed — both are registered in per-device DI.
  If their types conflict, raise ValueError at registration.

- **enabled= parameter**: Applied to all devices from the dict. For per-device
  enabled, use @app.on_configure instead.

- **group= parameter**: All dict-registered devices can share a group. They all
  get the same group name.

- **publish= / persist=**: Shared across all dict-registered devices.

## Scope decisions

### v1 (this task):
- name: Callable[[Settings], dict[str, T]] on @app.telemetry
- Per-device config injection via DI (dict values registered by type)

title: Implement adapter restart logic in health check runner
description:
Implement the adapter restart mechanism triggered by consecutive health check failures.

## Requirements

1. Extend HealthCheckRunner (from Epic 5) with restart logic:
   - After each health check failure, check if consecutive_failures >= restart_after_failures
   - If threshold reached and total_restarts < max_restarts, trigger restart

2. Restart procedure:
   ```python
   async def _restart_adapter(self, port_type: type, adapter: T) -> None:
       logger.warning("Restarting adapter %s after %d consecutive failures",
                      port_type.__name__, self._status[port_type].consecutive_failures)
       # 1. Cancel device tasks using this adapter
       for device_task in self._get_device_tasks(port_type):
           device_task.cancel()
       await asyncio.gather(*device_tasks, return_exceptions=True)
       
       # 2. Exit adapter lifecycle
       await adapter.__aexit__(None, None, None)
       
       # 3. Cooldown
       await asyncio.sleep(self._restart_cooldown)
       
       # 4. Re-enter adapter lifecycle
       await adapter.__aenter__()
       
       # 5. Re-create and start device tasks
       await self._recreate_device_tasks(port_type)
       
       # 6. Reset counters
       self._status[port_type].consecutive_failures = 0
       self._status[port_type].total_restarts += 1
   ```

3. Error handling during restart:
   - If __aexit__ raises: log ERROR, continue to __aenter__ attempt
   - If __aenter__ raises: log CRITICAL, mark adapter as permanently offline,
     do not attempt further restarts

4. Add parameters to App constructor:
   - restart_after_failures: int = 5 (0 to disable auto-restart)
   - max_restarts: int = 3
   - restart_cooldown: float = 5.0

5. Track restart state in AdapterHealthStatus (extend from Epic 5):
   - total_restarts: int
   - last_restart: float | None
   - restart_exhausted: bool

- packages/src/cosalette/_health.py — Extend HealthCheckRunner + AdapterHealthStatus
- packages/src/cosalette/_app.py — Add restart params, wire device task recreation
- packages/src/cosalette/_adapter_lifecycle.py — Expose exit/re-enter methods

title: Implement device task cancellation and recreation after adapter restart
description:
Implement the mechanism to cancel device tasks using a restarted adapter and recreate
them after the adapter is back online.

## Requirements

1. Build adapter→device_task mapping during wiring phase:
   - For each device, record which adapter port types it depends on
   - Store in HealthCheckRunner or a shared registry

2. Cancel device tasks:
   - task.cancel() for each affected device task
   - await asyncio.gather(*tasks, return_exceptions=True) to clean up
   - Log which device tasks are being cancelled

3. Recreate device tasks:
   - Re-run the wiring phase for affected devices only
   - Re-invoke init= callbacks (they may depend on the fresh adapter)
   - Start new asyncio tasks for the recreated devices
   - New DeviceContext created (old one is stale)

4. State implications (document clearly):
   - @app.device handlers lose their loop state (closures, local variables)
   - DeviceStore data survives (persisted to disk)
   - Telemetry handlers are stateless by design, so restart is seamless
   - Command handlers may lose in-flight state
   - Document this trade-off in the ADR and reference docs

5. Edge case: device depends on multiple adapters, only one restarts
   - Cancel the device task (it can't function with one adapter down)
   - Recreate after the restarting adapter is back

## Files to modify

- packages/src/cosalette/_app.py — Device task lifecycle management
- packages/src/cosalette/_wiring.py — Per-device adapter dependency tracking
- packages/src/cosalette/_health.py — Trigger recreation from restart logic

title: ADR: Adapter auto-restart strategy
description:
Write ADR for adapter auto-restart on health check failure.

## ⚠️ USER INPUT REQUIRED — present these trade-offs before writing the ADR

### Decision 1: Device task handling during restart
What happens to device tasks when the adapter restarts?

| Option | Behavior | Pros | Cons |
|--------|----------|------|------|
| A: Cancel + recreate | Cancel running tasks, recreate after restart | Clean state, no stale references | Loses @app.device loop state, closures, local variables |
| B: Suspend + resume | Set a "paused" flag, device loop checks it | Preserves loop state | Complex — device must cooperate (check flag); adapter reference may be stale |
| C: Replace adapter ref | Swap adapter reference in DI, devices keep running | Minimal disruption | Thread safety concerns; device may hold stale adapter handle |

**Recommendation:** Option A — cancel + recreate. This is the simplest and most
predictable. DeviceStore data survives (persisted). @app.telemetry handlers are
stateless by design so restart is seamless. Only @app.device handlers lose state.
**Ask user:** Is losing @app.device loop state acceptable? For velux2mqtt, this
means the PositionTracker, DriftCompensator, and CalibrationStateMachine would
be recreated from scratch. DeviceStore could persist position, but calibration
state would be lost. Is this acceptable given that adapter restart means the
hardware had a failure anyway?

### Decision 2: Max restarts reset condition
After max_restarts is reached, the adapter stays offline permanently (until
container restart). Should max_restarts reset after a period of sustained health?

| Option | Behavior |
|--------|----------|
| A: Never reset | max_restarts is a hard lifetime limit |
| B: Reset after sustained_health_duration (e.g., 5 minutes) | Allows recovery from intermittent failures |

**Recommendation:** Option B — reset after 5 minutes of consecutive healthy checks.
This handles the case where a BLE adapter has rare failures days apart.
**Ask user:** Is 5 minutes a reasonable default? Should it be configurable?

### Decision 3: Restart cooldown
How long to wait between __aexit__ and __aenter__?

**Recommendation:** 5 seconds default, configurable via App(restart_cooldown=5.0).
For BLE adapters, the Bluetooth daemon may need a few seconds to release resources.
**Ask user:** Is 5s reasonable? Any adapter that needs more or less?

### Decision 4: Should restart be opt-in per adapter?
- **All HealthCheckable adapters auto-restart** (if health_check_interval > 0 and
  restart_after_failures > 0)
- **Per-adapter opt-in:** adapter must also implement Restartable protocol or
  set a flag

**Recommendation:** All HealthCheckable adapters with lifecycle methods (__aenter__/
__aexit__) auto-restart. If an adapter has health_check() but no lifecycle, it
can't be restarted (logged as WARNING). No separate opt-in needed.
**Ask user:** Is implicit restart acceptable? Some adapters might not survive
exit+re-enter (e.g., hardware that can't be re-initialized). Should there be
an opt-out?

### Decision 5: What happens to in-flight commands during restart?
If a command arrives while the adapter is restarting:
- **Drop it** (command is lost)
- **Queue it** and deliver after restart
- **Reject it** (publish error to error topic)

**Recommendation:** Queue commands during restart, deliver after devices are
recreated. Commands are asynchronous by nature — a few seconds delay is acceptable.
**Ask user:** Preference?

- packages/src/cosalette/_health.py (health check runner from Epic 5)
- packages/src/cosalette/_app.py (_run_async device task management)

title: Epic 6: Adapter Auto-Restart on Health Check Failure
description:
When an adapter's health check fails consecutively beyond a threshold, automatically
restart the adapter (exit + re-enter lifecycle) and resume device tasks.

## Motivation

Epic 5 detects unhealthy adapters and reports availability, but operators still must
manually restart the container. Auto-restart closes the loop: detect → restart → recover
automatically for transient adapter failures (BlueZ wedge, serial port glitch).

## Scope

- Configurable restart threshold: restart_after_failures (default: 5)
- Configurable max restarts: max_restarts (default: 3, to prevent restart loops)
- On threshold reached: call adapter.__aexit__, then __aenter__ again
- After restart: reset health check counter, resume device tasks
- If max_restarts exhausted: log CRITICAL, keep adapter offline, don't restart again
- Restart is logged at WARNING with adapter type and failure count
- Cooldown between restarts (prevent rapid restart loops)
- ADR, tests, docs

## Dependencies

- Depends on Epic 5 (COS-497) for HealthCheckable protocol and consecutive_failures

## Apps affected

- airthings2mqtt: BLE adapter auto-restart
- jeelink2mqtt: serial adapter auto-restart
- velux2mqtt: GPIO adapter auto-restart
- vito2mqtt: serial adapter auto-restart

title: ADR: Adapter health check protocol design
description:
Write ADR for the adapter health check protocol.

## ⚠️ USER INPUT REQUIRED — present these trade-offs before writing the ADR

### Decision 1: Health check interval — global or per-adapter?

| Option | API | Pros | Cons |
|--------|-----|------|------|
| A: Global only | App(health_check_interval=30) | Simple, one setting | BLE adapter may need 60s, serial 10s |
| B: Per-adapter override | App(health_check_interval=30) + adapter-level override | Flexible | How to configure per-adapter? Extra API surface |
| C: Protocol method | health_check_interval() -> float on the adapter itself | Self-contained, adapter knows best | Framework can't control it; hard to override in settings |

**Recommendation:** Option A for v1 — global interval. Per-adapter can be added
later. The interval doesn't need to be precise (30s vs 60s doesn't matter much
for health detection).
**Ask user:** Is a global 30s default acceptable for all adapter types (BLE, serial,
GPIO)? Any adapter where 30s is too frequent or too slow?

### Decision 2: What does the framework do when health_check() returns False?
- Set availability to "offline" for affected devices (definitely)
- Should it also **pause telemetry polling** for those devices? (saves error log noise)

| Option | Behavior | Pros | Cons |
|--------|----------|------|------|
| A: Availability only | Set offline, telemetry continues (and fails) | Simple, telemetry errors are informational | Log noise from expected failures |
| B: Availability + pause telemetry | Set offline, skip telemetry calls until healthy | Clean logs, no wasted cycles | More complex, telemetry "misses" are silent |

**Recommendation:** Option A for v1 — health check is informational. Pausing
telemetry is a form of "acting on health" that belongs in Epic 6 (auto-restart).
Keep this epic focused on detection + reporting.
**Ask user:** Is log noise from failing telemetry during unhealthy adapter
acceptable? The error deduplication already suppresses consecutive identical errors.

### Decision 3: Health check for adapters without __aenter__/__aexit__
Some adapters are stateless (no lifecycle). Should they be health-checkable?

**Recommendation:** Yes — HealthCheckable is independent from adapter lifecycle.
An adapter can implement health_check() without __aenter__/__aexit__. The framework
calls health_check() regardless of lifecycle support.
**Ask user:** Confirm. This matters for Epic 6 — auto-restart only works for
adapters with lifecycle methods.

### Decision 4: Adapter→device mapping granularity
How does the framework know which devices depend on which adapter?

| Option | Mechanism | Pros | Cons |
|--------|-----------|------|------|
| A: Inspect DI resolution | Track which adapter types each device handler requests | Automatic, no user config | Requires DI introspection at wiring time |
| B: Explicit mapping | App(adapter_devices={BlePort: ["sensor_a", "sensor_b"]}) | Clear | Manual, error-prone |

**Recommendation:** Option A — the DI system already knows which types each
handler requests. Build the mapping during device wiring automatically.
**Ask user:** Confirm automatic mapping is preferred.

### Decision 5: Health check during startup
Should the framework run an initial health check before starting device tasks?
- **Yes:** Devices start with accurate availability from the beginning
- **No:** Availability starts as "online" (existing behavior), first health check
  runs after health_check_interval seconds

**Recommendation:** Yes — run one check during startup, before device tasks.
If it fails, devices still start (availability just starts as "offline").
**Ask user:** Should startup health check failure be a WARNING or prevent device startup?

title: Epic 5: Adapter Health Check / Readiness Probe
description:
Add an optional health_check() protocol method for adapters. When implemented, the
framework periodically calls it and toggles per-device availability accordingly.

## Motivation

BLE adapters can enter a wedged state (BlueZ daemon crash, adapter hardware reset) where
connections fail indefinitely. The framework's availability topic stays "online" even when
the adapter is non-functional. Operators must notice repeated errors in logs and manually
restart the container.

## Scope

- HealthCheckable Protocol: async def health_check(self) -> bool
- Framework detects adapters implementing the protocol via isinstance check
- Periodic health check loop (configurable interval, default 30s)
- On failure: set device availability to "offline", log WARNING
- On recovery: set device availability back to "online", log INFO
- Consecutive failures counted for the auto-restart epic (Epic 6)
- ADR, tests, docs

## Out of scope (see Epic 6)

- Automatic adapter restart on health check failure
- Adapter reconnection logic

## Apps affected

title: ADR: Lifespan-yielded DI state design
description:
Write ADR for lifespan-yielded injectable state.

## ⚠️ USER INPUT REQUIRED — present these trade-offs before writing the ADR

### Decision 1: How to determine the DI registration type
When the lifespan yields a value, what type key is used for DI?

| Option | Mechanism | Pros | Cons |
|--------|-----------|------|------|
| A: type(yielded_value) at runtime | Inspect the actual object | Simple, always works | Can't inject by Protocol/ABC — only concrete type |
| B: Return annotation of lifespan function | Inspect AsyncIterator[SharedState] | Supports abstract types | Fragile with generics, forward refs |
| C: Explicit parameter on App() | lifespan_type=SharedState | No magic | Verbose boilerplate |

**Recommendation:** Option A — use type(yielded_value). This is what FastAPI does.
If the user wants to inject by a Protocol type, they can use a wrapper.
**Ask user:** Is injecting by concrete type sufficient? Or do any apps need to
yield a Protocol/ABC type?

### Decision 2: Breaking change on LifespanFunc type alias
Current: Callable[[AppContext], AbstractAsyncContextManager[None]]
New: Callable[[AppContext], AbstractAsyncContextManager[T | None]]

This is a **type-level breaking change** — existing lifespans that yield None will
still work at runtime, but type checkers may flag the change.
- **Option A:** Change the type alias (minor breakage for type-strict users)
- **Option B:** Keep old alias, add new LifespanWithStateFunc alias
- **Option C:** Accept both via Union in App() constructor type hint

**Recommendation:** Option A — the runtime behavior is backward-compatible.
Type-checking breakage is acceptable in a minor version bump since None satisfies
T | None.
**Ask user:** Is the type alias breakage acceptable?

### Decision 3: What if yielded type matches an adapter port type?
E.g., lifespan yields an object whose type happens to match a registered adapter.
- **Option A:** RuntimeError at startup with clear message
- **Option B:** Lifespan value takes precedence (overrides adapter)
- **Option C:** Adapter takes precedence (lifespan value ignored)

**Recommendation:** Option A — conflict is an error. Clear and predictable.
**Ask user:** Confirm.

### Decision 4: Availability of yielded state in on_configure hooks
If Epic 1 lands first, on_configure hooks run before lifespan (lifespan is in the
Run phase, on_configure is in the Wire phase). Should we change the lifecycle to
run lifespan before on_configure?

Current lifecycle: ... Adapters → [on_configure] → Wire → **Lifespan** → Devices
If lifespan runs before on_configure: ... Adapters → **Lifespan** → [on_configure] → Wire → Devices

**Recommendation:** Keep current order — lifespan runs after on_configure.
Yielded state is NOT available in on_configure hooks. This is a documented
constraint. If an on_configure hook needs shared state, use module-level setup.
**Ask user:** Is this acceptable, or should lifespan move earlier?

## After user approval, write ADR

## Context files

- packages/src/cosalette/_app.py (lifespan handling in _run_async)
- packages/src/cosalette/_injection.py (DI registration)
- jeelink2mqtt app.py (SharedState singleton pattern to replace)

title: Implement lifespan yield capture and DI registration
description:
Capture the value yielded by lifespan and register it in the DI system.

## Requirements

1. In _run_async(), when entering the lifespan context manager:
   ```python

       if state is not None:
           self._di_registry[type(state)] = state
   ```
2. Update LifespanFunc type alias to allow yielding non-None values
3. Yielded value available to all device handlers, init= callbacks, and on_configure hooks
4. If type(state) is already registered in DI (e.g., it's Settings), raise RuntimeError
5. On lifespan exit (teardown), remove the type from DI registry
6. Update __init__.py exports: update LifespanFunc type alias

title: Epic 4: Lifespan-Yielded Injectable State
description:
Enable lifespan hooks to yield a value that is automatically registered in the DI
system, following the FastAPI lifespan pattern.

## Motivation

jeelink2mqtt uses a module-level singleton (_state: SharedState | None = None) set
during lifespan because there is no DI-friendly way to create shared state in lifespan
and inject it into device handlers. The module-global pattern is untestable and fragile.

## Scope

- Change LifespanFunc type alias to support AsyncIterator[T] (yield instead of None)
- Framework captures yielded value and registers it in DI by its type
- Device handlers can then declare the type as a parameter to receive it
- Backward compatible: lifespan yielding None continues to work
- ADR, tests, docs

## Apps affected

- jeelink2mqtt: SharedState singleton → lifespan-yielded (direct beneficiary)
- vito2mqtt, gas2mqtt: potential shared initialization state
- airthings2mqtt: potential connection pool caching

title: Fix stale --show-devices rows in docs/concepts/introspection.md Use Cases table
description:
The "Use Cases" table in docs/concepts/introspection.md (lines 169-174) misdescribes both introspection CLI flags as rendering the registry snapshot. Both actually render AsyncAPI.

Verified against packages/src/cosalette/_cli.py:

- Line 171 claims "--show-devices flag renders the snapshot as a table". _cli.py:196 actually calls format_asyncapi_table(app.asyncapi()).
- Line 172 claims "--show-devices-json dumps as JSON". _cli.py:191 actually does json.dumps(app.asyncapi(), indent=2) — also AsyncAPI, not the snapshot.

So the defect is broader than the single row: the whole table presents the two flags as consumers of build_registry_snapshot(), which they are not. The surrounding page is genuinely about the registry snapshot, which is what makes the claim convincing and wrong — a reader would expect --show-devices output to match the snapshot structure documented above it.

Also check the comments at introspection.md:185 and :188 ("used by --show-devices" / "used by --show-devices-json") next to format_registry_table / format_registry_json — those attribute the snapshot formatters to the same flags and are stale for the same reason.

Note this is a pre-existing issue, explicitly called out as NOT fixed in PR #366 (scope). Not covered by cos-rzrm, which is scoped to _ai_content/_help_extra.py, nor by cos-mur.2 or cos-f4g.7, which add content to this page rather than correcting these rows.

Worth considering as part of the fix: whether the flags are misnamed/misplaced rather than the docs being wrong — i.e. whether --show-devices *should* render the snapshot. If so, this becomes a CLI bug rather than a docs fix, and should be re-filed accordingly.
acceptance_criteria:
The Use Cases table in docs/concepts/introspection.md correctly states that --show-devices and --show-devices-json render AsyncAPI, not the registry snapshot.
The stale "used by --show-devices" / "used by --show-devices-json" comments in the Formatting section are corrected or removed.
The page makes clear how to actually obtain the registry snapshot from the CLI (or states that there is no flag for it).
A decision is recorded on whether the docs were wrong or the flags are, and the issue re-filed as a CLI bug if the latter.
close_reason: Fixed docs/concepts/introspection.md: Use Cases table and Formatting-section comments now correctly attribute --show-devices/--show-devices-json to format_asyncapi_table(app.asyncapi())/json.dumps(app.asyncapi()), not the registry snapshot. Added an explicit note that no cosalette CLI flag currently renders the registry snapshot (cosalette_inspect_app MCP tool or build_registry_snapshot()/format_registry_table()/format_registry_json() are the actual ways to get it). Judgment call: docs were wrong, flags are not misnamed (format_asyncapi_table groups AsyncAPI channels by device/telemetry/command archetype, so 'show devices as a table' is a reasonable description) -- not re-filed as a CLI bug. Commit ab1f8c6.

title: Add stream channels to AsyncAPI as a fourth x-cosalette-archetype (needs ADR)
description:
Why this issue exists:
`@app.stream` and `@app.periodic` registrations are deliberately absent from the
emitted AsyncAPI document. The exclusion was justified in the 2026-08-07 additive
amendment to ADR-045 (stateful stream receiver semantics), filed alongside the work
that made `state_model` load-bearing (cos-v1dj.1 / cos-v1dj.2). Stream and periodic
metadata currently surfaces only via the registry snapshot.

That was the right call for that PR, but it leaves AsyncAPI an incomplete picture of
the app. This bead tracks doing it properly as a fourth archetype.

Requires its own ADR:
Do not implement this without an accepted ADR — the exclusion is a recorded decision
in ADR-045's amendment, so reversing/extending it needs a decision record. Use the
`adr-create` skill (`task adr:create`); do not hand-write ADR Markdown.

Blocker 1 — `x-cosalette-archetype` is a closed `Literal`:
- `packages/src/cosalette/_schema/__init__.py:173` and `:187` both declare
  `archetype: Literal["telemetry", "command", "device"] | None = None`.
- `packages/src/cosalette/_schema/_loader_helpers.py:75` validates membership
  against the same closed set `{"telemetry", "command", "device"}` and appends a
  load error otherwise.
Adding `"stream"` means touching all three sites, and the two `Literal`s must stay
in sync with the loader's runtime set.

Blocker 2 — schema-loader backward compatibility:
Older readers reject an unknown archetype outright (see the loader error path
above), so a document containing `x-cosalette-archetype: stream` will fail to load
on any previously released version. The ADR needs a compatibility story, e.g.:
- version-gate emission so stream channels only appear when the consumer opts in;
- make the loader forward-tolerant (warn-and-skip unknown archetypes) *first*, ship
  that, and only emit `"stream"` once tolerant loaders are the floor;
- or accept the break and document it as a breaking schema change.
Whichever is chosen, it has to be explicit — this is the reason the exclusion
existed.

Blocker 3 — `schema ha-discovery` side effect:
AsyncAPI also drives `schema ha-discovery`. Adding stream channels to AsyncAPI would
cause new Home Assistant entities to be created silently on the next regeneration,
for apps whose authors never asked for HA entities for their streams. The ADR must
address this — either exclude the `stream` archetype from ha-discovery generation,
require an opt-in, or define and document the intended entity mapping. Shipping the
archetype without settling this would surprise existing deployments.

Also worth deciding:
- Whether `@app.periodic` gets the same treatment or a separate archetype (it has no
  channel/address in the MQTT sense).
- What `address_template` and operation shape a stream channel should have, given
  `_device_name_from_archetype` (`_schema/__init__.py:299`) infers device names from
  archetype channels with 3+ segments.

Reference: ADR-045, 2026-08-07 additive amendment ("AsyncAPI deliberately
excluded").
acceptance_criteria:
An ADR is created via `task adr:create` and accepted, superseding or extending ADR-045's 2026-08-07 amendment that excluded stream channels from AsyncAPI.
`x-cosalette-archetype` accepts `"stream"`: both Literal declarations (_schema/__init__.py:173, :187) and the loader validation set (_schema/_loader_helpers.py:75) are updated consistently.
A backward-compatibility story for older schema loaders is implemented and documented — older readers must not silently break on a document containing the new archetype.
The `schema ha-discovery` side effect is addressed: new stream channels do not silently create Home Assistant entities on regeneration.
A decision is recorded on whether @app.periodic is covered by the same archetype, a separate one, or stays excluded.
Tests cover emission, round-trip loading, the compatibility path, and the ha-discovery behaviour.
close_reason: Stream AsyncAPI archetype implemented per ADR-054 across all phases

title: Sweep _ai_content/_help_extra.py for stale API-surface claims
description:
`_ai_content/_help_extra.py` documents the framework's API surface for the
`cosalette ai help` topics. Because it is hand-maintained prose rather than
generated from signatures, it can drift out of sync with the real API and then
confidently describe parameters that do not exist.

Concrete instance found while working cos-v1dj: the `Router` topic documented a
`lifespan=` parameter that `Router.__init__` has never accepted. A reader
following the help text would write code that raises `TypeError`.

This is a class of defect, not a one-off — the same file also had to be touched
when `dependencies=` was removed from `Router` (cos-v1dj.3). Task: audit every
API claim in `_help_extra.py` against the actual signatures and fix the stale
ones.

Worth considering as part of the fix: a test that reflects over the documented
parameter names for each topic and asserts they exist on the corresponding
callable, so this drift becomes a CI failure rather than a reader's problem.
close_reason: Audited every API-surface claim in _ai_content/_help_extra.py against current signatures (Router, App.include_router, Depends, Payload, Topic, consumer/temperature/percent, DeviceStore, TriggerPayload, sub-entity rules). lifespan=/dependencies= claims were already fixed by cos-v1dj.3 (#365). Found and fixed one remaining defect: the react topic's 'Testing Reactors' example used a nonexistent FakeDeviceContext() and MemoryStore().device_store(), and asserted on a nonexistent ctx.published attribute -- replaced with the real cosalette.testing device_context/mock_mqtt pytest fixtures and DeviceStore(MemoryStore(), ...). Added packages/tests/unit/ai_content/test_help_extra_api_drift.py: a lightweight reflection test asserting a curated set of documented parameter names exist on the real callables/TypedDict, plus regression guards for the lifespan=/dependencies= defect class. Commit c035abb.

title: uv.lock version drift forces UV_FROZEN=1 on every commit
description:
`pyproject.toml` declares version 0.5.10 but the committed `uv.lock` still
records 0.5.9. Any pre-commit hook that shells out to `uv run` (notably
`detect-secrets`) therefore resolves the project, rewrites `uv.lock`
0.5.9 -> 0.5.10 mid-hook, and pre-commit then fails the run with
"files were modified by this hook".

The practical consequence is that every commit in this repo currently has to be
made as `UV_FROZEN=1 git commit ...`. Contributors who do not know this hit an
opaque failure and are tempted to reach for `--no-verify`.

Two candidate fixes:

1. Commit the lock bump so `uv.lock` matches `pyproject.toml` (0.5.10). Likely
   the release-please flow should be doing this already — worth checking why the
   0.5.10 release commit did not include the regenerated lock.
2. Set `UV_FROZEN=1` in the affected pre-commit hook entries (or repo-wide in
   the hook environment) so hooks can never mutate the lock.

Option 2 is defence in depth and is worth doing regardless of 1, since the drift
can recur on the next version bump.
close_reason: Fixed: regenerated uv.lock via task sync to match pyproject.toml's 0.5.10 (it was already there in the working tree, just needed a proper commit). Added UV_FROZEN=1 defense-in-depth (via a bash -c wrapper, since pre-commit local hooks don't support env:) to both uv-run-based hooks: detect-secrets and ty. Verified fix by committing normally without UV_FROZEN=1 git commit — pre-commit hooks ran clean, uv.lock untouched. Note: the working-tree .secrets.baseline modification (empty results, dropping 3 pre-existing unverified findings) present at task start was investigated and could not be reproduced via any legitimate detect-secrets-hook or scan invocation against the pre-existing 3 files it flags (Dockerfile, _errors.py, test_errors.py) -- discarded as unexplained noise, reverted to match HEAD. Commit bd3c7b5.

title: DI robustness polish
description:
Why this issue exists:
An umbrella for the smaller dependency-injection sharp edges found during the
documentation audit. None is individually blocking; together they account for most
of the surprising DI behaviour.

Re-scoped 2026-08-07: one item is done and one has been split out (see below), so
what remains here is genuinely P3 polish — three diagnostics/validation
improvements with no open design questions.

Remaining scope:

• Detect ambiguous provider matches. `_find_subclass_instance`
  (`_injection.py:369-380`) silently returns the first `issubclass` match in dict
  order, so `def h(p: object)` silently receives whatever is first — in a real app,
  the `DeviceContext`. Should raise instead of picking dict order.

• Tighten marker validation: scan all `Annotated` metadata rather than only
  `args[1]`; error on multiple binding markers instead of silently dropping the
  extras; reject `Topic()` on a non-`str` inner type.

• Improve the generic-annotation error message (`_injection.py:192-199`) to redirect
  to `Annotated[T, Payload()]`. ADR-046:30 advertises generic mappings and sequences
  as supported, so the current "use a concrete type" advice is the wrong fix.

DONE — no longer in scope:

• ~~Support callable-object dependencies under PEP 563/649 by extending
  `_hint_source_for` to use `type(obj).__call__` for instances.~~ Fully implemented
  and tested as part of cos-v1dj.4 (closed), in PR #364
  (`fix/di-diagnostics-cos-v1dj`). `_hint_source_for` now substitutes
  `type(obj).__call__` for callable instances so PEP 563 annotations resolve against
  the correct module globals; covered by `TestHintSourceFor` in
  `packages/tests/unit/injection/test_injection.py`. Note PR #364 is open at the
  time of this re-scope, so the code lands with that PR rather than being on `main`
  already — nothing further is needed here either way.

SPLIT OUT — tracked separately:

• The `T | None` optional-injection item moved to cos-o6c4 (linked as related). It
  is not polish: it is an API design question — what *should* injecting an optional
  dependency mean when no provider is registered? — and it needs an ADR before
  implementation. It was blocking this bead from being a clean P3 sweep.
acceptance_criteria:
Ambiguous provider matches raise rather than silently picking dict order.
Marker validation covers all Annotated metadata, errors on multiple binding markers, and rejects invalid Topic() inner types.
The generic-annotation error redirects to Annotated[T, Payload()] rather than advising a concrete type.
(Removed: callable-object hint resolution — done in cos-v1dj.4 / PR #364. Removed: the T | None decision — split out to cos-o6c4, which needs an ADR.)

title: Add --exclude scripts/setup-github-remote.sh to update:template
description:
Copier re-creates `scripts/setup-github-remote.sh` on **every** update, regardless of the `create_remote_repo: false` answer.

## Root cause (verified against template v1.19.2)

- `template/scripts/setup-github-remote.sh.jinja` has **no** `{% if create_remote_repo %}` gate around its body.
- `copier.yml` has **no** `_exclude` entry for it.
- The answer only gates the post-copy task hook: `when: "{{ create_remote_repo and _copier_operation == 'copy' }}"` (copier.yml:164).

So the file itself is rendered unconditionally on `copier update`. It runs `gh repo create`, which is meaningless for a repo that has existed for months. It was deleted in cos-devm.11 and will come back on the next update.

## Fix

`Taskfile.yml`, task `update:template` (~line 350):

```yaml
update:template:
  desc: Update project from copier template (pulls latest template changes)
  cmds:
    - uvx --python 3.14 --with jinja2-time copier update --trust
        --exclude scripts/setup-github-remote.sh
```

Apply the same flag to `update:template:pr` (~line 368), which invokes copier directly.

Verify `copier update --exclude` is accepted by the pinned copier version before relying on it; if the flag only applies to `copy`, fall back to a post-update `rm -f` in the task.

## Better long-term fix

Upstream in `ff-fab/tmpl_python_project_kickstart`: wrap the jinja template in a `create_remote_repo` conditional or add `_exclude`. Worth an upstream issue.

## Context

Recorded in `docs/maintenance/copier-template-divergence.md` (section "Copier itself"); update that page when this lands.

## Acceptance

- `task update:template` no longer re-creates `scripts/setup-github-remote.sh`
- Both `update:template` and `update:template:pr` carry the flag
- Drift doc updated

comments.author: Fabian Koerner
comments.text:
Second file needs the same treatment: .github/workflows/docs-preview.yml

Discovered during cos-devm.13. The surge_token answer was corrected false -> true in this epic (18d93d0). In template v1.19.2 that answer gates exactly one thing -- the filename
template/.github/workflows/{% if surge_token %}docs-preview.yml{% endif %}.jinja
(verified: docs.yml.jinja never references surge_token, so it renders the GitHub Pages version either way).

Consequence: every future 'copier update' will now render a NEW .github/workflows/docs-preview.yml that this repo does not have and does not want -- cosalette already implements PR previews and teardown as the deploy-preview and teardown jobs inside docs.yml. Keeping both would double-deploy to the same cosalette-pr-<N>.surge.sh domain.

So the fix here should exclude both paths:

  copier update --trust \
    --exclude scripts/setup-github-remote.sh \

description:

title: Implement settings-resolving schema dump mode (ADR-051)
description:
Step (c) of the epic. ADR-051 (Accepted, 2026-08-04) chose Option 1: a
settings-resolving schema dump mode that resolves settings and runs the
configure + expand phases (including the same `expand_name_specs()` used at
bootstrap) before calling `build_app_asyncapi()`, so the static AsyncAPI
artifact contains post-expansion, concrete entity names that match the
runtime name set by construction. This is what actually unblocks per-entity
HA discovery for settings-derived apps (velux2mqtt, caldates2mqtt, and
jeelink2mqtt if it moves to registered entities).

The design gate is closed; implementation is still pending (tracked here).
See docs/adr/ADR-051-settings-aware-schema-pipeline-for-settings-derived-entity-names.md
for full context, considered options, and consequences.

Interim safety net already shipped (cos-sdne.1/cos-sdne.2): schema
dump/init/check fail loudly on unexpanded NameSpecs instead of silently
emitting phantom/missing discovery payloads.

Operational stopgap that still works today: the post-expansion AsyncAPI
document is published retained to {prefix}/_meta/registry
(_wiring/_infra.py:246, built from app.asyncapi() at :252, after expansion),
and schema ha-discovery accepts a file path (_schema/_cli.py:349), so
"mosquitto_sub -C 1 -t /_meta/registry > /tmp/app.json" followed by
"cosalette schema ha-discovery /tmp/app.json" yields correct per-entity
payloads. That remains a deployment stopgap, not a substitute for this
implementation.
close_reason: Implemented as opt-in --resolve-settings/--env-file flags on schema dump (commit 64d69df). init/check remain import-time-only; follow-up if per-entity discovery validation is needed there too.

title: Deferred (F5): relocatable MCP command + per-tool (--claude/--kilo) MCP targets
description: Deferred from cosalette-apps enhancement proposal (Finding 5). Two parts: (a) _manage_mcp_config() writes .vscode/mcp.json using sys.executable — an absolute interpreter path that is only valid for one checkout location (breaks on other clone paths / host checkouts). (b) MCP config is VS Code-only; Claude Code (mcpServers in .mcp.json) and Kilo (mcp block in kilo.jsonc, type: local|remote) are written by hand. Proposed: emit a relocatable command (e.g. uv run --package cosalette python -m cosalette ai mcp serve, or python3 -m cosalette resolved via active env) and add per-tool MCP targets via --claude/--kilo. Deferred because the right relocatable command is genuinely debatable and downstream (cosalette-apps) accepted current behavior as a devcontainer-only constraint; needs design before implementation.

title: schema generator: emit unicode consumer values unescaped and preserve consumer() call order
description: cosalette schema init/dump serializes non-ASCII x-cosalette-consumer values as escaped sequences (unit: "\xB0C", "Bq/m\xB3") and orders consumer metadata keys alphabetically instead of consumer() call order. This degrades readability of published zensical docs artifacts across every model-driven app (airthings2mqtt, wallpanel-control, gas2mqtt, vito2mqtt, velux2mqtt). The model->schema mapping is correct; this is a docs-quality/cosmetic fix that lives in the framework's YAML emitter and json-schema generator. Fix: (1) dump YAML with allow_unicode=True; (2) preserve insertion order of x-cosalette-consumer keys via a GenerateJsonSchema subclass that skips sorting under that key. Discovered in cosalette-apps pr-review of cap-3mb (PR #184), maintainability finding #5 (INFO).
notes: Fixed in _schema/_asyncapi.py (order-preserving GenerateJsonSchema subclass wired into _type_to_json_schema) and _schema/_cli.py (allow_unicode=True on all four schema-doc YAML dumps: dump, init, slice, ha-discovery yaml). Consumer keys now keep consumer() call order; all other schema keys stay alphabetically sorted for stable diffs. Tests added in tests/unit/schema/test_schema_cli.py::TestConsumerMetadataDocsQuality. Apps must regenerate docs/schema.yaml to pick up the cosmetic improvement.
close_reason: Implemented in fix/schema-unicode-consumer-order; PR to follow.

title: Flaky Hypothesis test: MedianFilter test_output_bounded_by_window intermittently fails in CI
description:
packages/tests/unit/filters/test_filters_properties.py::TestMedianFilterProperties::test_output_bounded_by_window failed once in CI on an unrelated PR (#349, run 30080150628) and passed on a --failed re-run. It passes locally under random Hypothesis seeds (200 examples). Classic flaky property test: a rare counterexample surfaces only under some seeds/example-DB states.

The test asserts, for each update, min(active) <= result <= max(active) where active = buf[-window:] and result = MedianFilter(window).update(v). Strategies: values=sensor_sequences (lists 1..200 of floats in [-1e6,1e6], no NaN/inf), window=int 1..50. MedianFilter is the Rust extension cosalette._filters_rs (not Python), so this exercises the Rust impl.

Suspected root cause (needs confirmation): even-window median interpolation. If the Rust filter returns the average of the two middle elements for even window sizes, floating-point rounding of (a+b)/2 is mathematically within [min,max] — so that alone should not break the bound. More likely a Rust/Python model mismatch in how the active window is tracked during fill (first <window updates), a tie/duplicate ordering edge, or a specific float where selection lands just outside the naive buf[-window:] model. The invariant itself is sound; the discrepancy is between the test's Python window model and the Rust filter's internal window semantics.
design: Repro/fix plan: (1) Recover the failing example — re-run CI job 30080150628 logs or add a printed repr on failure; or run locally with high volume: uv run pytest <nodeid> -p no:cov --hypothesis-seed=random with max_examples bumped to ~5000, and enable the Hypothesis example database in CI so counterexamples persist. (2) Once reproduced, decide whether it's a test-model bug (align buf[-window:] model with the Rust filter's fill/window semantics) or a genuine Rust MedianFilter edge case (fix the crate). (3) Add the minimized example as an explicit @example(...) regression case. (4) Consider pinning derandomize=True or a fixed seed for this test to keep CI deterministic while retaining coverage. Note: coverage is unaffected (92.13% in the failing run); this is purely test stability. Surfaced during PR #349 review.
notes: ROOT CAUSE CONFIRMED (not flaky — a real bug). Falsifying example from CI: values=[5e-324, 5e-324], window=2 → median returned 0.0, failing assert min([5e-324,5e-324]) <= 0.0. Bug is at crates/cosalette-filters-rs/src/median.rs:117 for the even-window branch: 'sorted[len/2-1] * 0.5 + sorted[len/2] * 0.5'. For subnormal inputs each half underflows (5e-324 * 0.5 rounds to 0.0), so the sum is 0.0 — outside [min,max]. Fix: use the interpolation form 'lo + (hi - lo) * 0.5' (lo=sorted[len/2-1], hi=sorted[len/2]); guarantees result in [lo,hi] with no underflow (b-a=0 for equal values) and no overflow for large bounded values. NOTE: local .venv ships a STALE compiled _filters_rs that still returns the correct value, so this only reproduces in a fresh Rust build (CI). The test is correct; the crate is wrong. Surfaced as a required-check blocker on PR #349 because Hypothesis cached the counterexample in CI's .cache/ and now replays it deterministically.
close_reason: Fixed: median.rs even-window midpoint now uses straddle-zero branching (lo+(hi-lo)*0.5 same-sign, (lo+hi)*0.5 across zero) — no subnormal underflow, no extreme overflow. Regression pinned via @example([5e-324,5e-324],2) + parametrized test_even_window_midpoint_is_robust. Root cause was a stale cpython-tagged .so masking it locally; CI builds fresh. Fixed within PR #349.

title: Gate: reject control characters in App(name=) to prevent log injection
description:
Pre-existing gap (CWE-117): validate_mqtt_name() allows CR/LF and other terminal control characters. The app name is embedded in log records via _warn_if_ephemeral_default_store() and in file paths, allowing a crafted name to forge or garble log entries.

Identified in PR #344 review (security-reviewer, MINOR).

Fix: extend the App name validator to reject ASCII control characters (0x00–0x1F, 0x7F). Simplest hook is validate_mqtt_name() in _registration.py.
close_reason: Fixed in PR #345 — control-char rejection in validate_mqtt_name and cross-platform store-path guard

title: Gate: cross-platform path safety for App(name=) in default store derivation
description:
Pre-existing security gap (OWASP A05 / CWE-22): validate_mqtt_name() rejects '/' but not '\', drive-qualified paths, or '..' segments. The package is declared OS-independent; on Windows a crafted App(name=...) can redirect the auto-created store.json outside the intended state directory.

Identified in PR #344 review (security-reviewer, MAJOR).

Fix: before deriving the store path in _store_defaults.py, reject any app name that is absolute or multi-part under PurePosixPath or PureWindowsPath, reject '.' and '..' segments after normalization, and reject control characters. Add cross-platform tests.
close_reason: Fixed in PR #345 — control-char rejection in validate_mqtt_name and cross-platform store-path guard

Current impl follows the proposal and uses values as-is (author-controlled, not external input). Consider stricter [^A-Z0-9_]->_ env normalization + path-safety guard. Deferred from ADR-049 core.

title: Clear orphaned retained topics for entities removed from config
description: Finding 2 / improvement idea (smoke test, framework-findings.md). The framework publishes RETAINED availability ({prefix}/{name}/availability) and state ({prefix}/{name}/state). When an entity is removed from config between restarts, its retained topics persist on the broker forever (observed: stale caldates2mqtt/birthday/availability=offline), confusing subscribers like Home Assistant. The framework should clear (empty retained publish) topics for entities present in a previous run but absent now, akin to HA MQTT discovery cleanup. Research (tmp research) found: broker enumeration is blocked by current MqttPort (no unsubscribe, no retained flag/end-of-burst signal); a store-backed previous-run snapshot works but only for apps with store= configured; dynamic sub-entities cannot be enumerated at startup; must run once on first connect (not every reconnect); shared prefixes are a hazard. No existing ADR. REQUIRES an ADR before implementation. Blocked on ADR acceptance.

title: Blank /set trigger payload should be equivalent to {}
description: F-1 (smoke test, framework-findings.md). A blank (empty or whitespace-only) MQTT payload to {prefix}/{device}/set for a triggerable=True telemetry device is the documented 'just re-run' trigger, but TriggerPayload.from_mqtt('') yields data=None while '{}' yields data={}. The typed Payload() path reads .raw, which is None for blank. Apps that branch on 'data is None' / typed 'Model | None' therefore no-op on a blank trigger. Fix: normalize a blank trigger payload to an empty JSON object in from_mqtt (data={}) and in the typed trigger branch (parse raw or '{}'), so a bare /set behaves identically to sending '{}'. Preserve the literal payload in .raw. Command-path payload parsing is unaffected (commands still require valid JSON). Update tests + telemetry-device.md docs.
close_reason: Implemented in a01ac98: from_mqtt normalizes blank trigger payloads to {}; typed trigger branch parses raw or {}. Tests + docs updated. Reviewed APPROVED.

title: F-2: per-device availability not re-emitted on reconnect
description: LOW (related to F-1). <prefix>/status is re-published on the ~60s heartbeat loop (heartbeat_loop in _wiring/_task_lifecycle.py), so it self-heals after an MQTT reconnect. The per-device <prefix>/<device>/availability topic is published only once and is NOT re-emitted on the heartbeat or on MQTT (re)connect, making availability the least reliable health signal. Subscribers connecting after a reconnect, or after a broker restart that dropped retained messages, see stale availability.
design: Reuse the MqttConnectAware connect-callback from F-1. On the FIRST connect: optimistic announce (online for all registrations) via _wiring.publish_device_availability. On RECONNECT: HealthReporter.reannounce() (new) publishes 'online' only for currently-tracked devices (root-aware), plus registry snapshot and heartbeat. reannounce() reuses _safe_publish (fire-and-forget). The wiring closure tracks first-vs-reconnect with a flag.
acceptance_criteria: On every successful MQTT (re)connect the framework re-asserts availability for currently-tracked (available) devices and re-publishes the registry snapshot and a heartbeat. Devices that transitioned offline keep their last retained 'offline'. Integration test (real Mosquitto, broker restart) shows availability returns to 'online' after reconnect; unit test with a connect-aware fake double proves reannounce fires on a simulated reconnect.

title: Pin devcontainer base image by digest
description:
## Context

The .devcontainer/Dockerfile uses a mutable tag for the base image:
FROM mcr.microsoft.com/devcontainers/python:3.14

Pinning by digest prevents supply-chain attacks where an attacker compromises a mutable tag.

## Scope
- Pin the base image to a full digest (e.g., @sha256:...)
- Configure Renovate to update the digest when new images are published
- Document the digest-pinning policy in deployment.md or an ADR if it becomes project-wide policy
- Ensure the weekly devcontainer build workflow still works with digest pinning

## References
- docs/guides/deployment.md already mentions digest pinning for production images
- ADR-008 (packaging and distribution) may need amendment if this becomes policy
- Related to cos-k6r (container scanning) but deferred for focused implementation
acceptance_criteria: Base image is pinned by digest. Renovate updates the digest automatically. Weekly builds work. Documentation reflects the policy.

title: Docs: add "Was this helpful?" feedback widget (AsyncAPI pattern)
description:
Analyze AsyncAPI's documentation user experience — specifically their "Was this helpful?" feedback tile — and implement an equivalent for the cosalette docs site.

## Background

AsyncAPI's documentation pages include a "Was this helpful?" widget at the bottom of each page, allowing readers to give quick thumbs-up/thumbs-down feedback on individual pages. This is a proven practice for identifying documentation gaps, confusing pages, and high-value content.

## Research Phase

1. **Analyze AsyncAPI's implementation** — visit [docs.asyncapi.com](https://www.asyncapi.com/docs) and document:
   - Widget placement, layout, and copy ("Was this helpful?", thumbs up/down, optional comment)
   - What happens after clicking (thank-you message, follow-up form, redirect?)
   - Where feedback is stored (GitHub issue? API? Google Analytics event? Posthog?)
   - Whether it's open-source / reusable (check their docs repo for the component)

2. **Survey other best practices** — briefly check how these docs handle feedback:
   - Material for MkDocs built-in `content.feedback` feature (already supported by the theme engine)
   - Stripe docs, Vercel docs, Tailwind docs feedback patterns
   - Identify which pattern fits best for a small OSS project (minimal infra, no backend)

## Design Decisions

1. **Backend/storage** — where does feedback go?
   - Option A: GitHub Issues (bot-created, labeled `docs-feedback`) — zero infra, transparent
   - Option B: GitHub Discussions — threaded, categorized, community-visible
   - Option C: Analytics event (plausible.io, simple-analytics, or GA4) — aggregate only, no PII
   - Option D: Material for MkDocs `content.feedback` with analytics integration — built-in theme support
   - Evaluate: which aligns with cosalette's infrastructure constraints (static site, no backend)?

2. **Widget design** — what to show:
   - Thumbs up / thumbs down (minimum viable)
   - Optional free-text follow-up on thumbs-down ("What was missing or confusing?")
   - Page context automatically captured (URL, title)
   - Thank-you confirmation after submission

3. **Scope** — which pages:
   - All docs pages? Guides only? Concepts + Guides?
   - Exclude auto-generated API reference?

## Implementation

1. **If using Zensical/Material built-in feature:**
   - Configure `content.feedback` in zensical.toml
   - Set up analytics provider integration (if needed)
   - Customize copy and icons via overrides

2. **If custom widget:**
   - Create partial template in overrides/ (e.g. `overrides/partials/feedback.html`)
   - CSS in `docs/assets/stylesheets/`
   - JS handler in `docs/javascripts/`
   - Wire into page template

3. **Test locally** with `task docs:serve`

## Acceptance Criteria

- "Was this helpful?" widget appears at the bottom of docs pages
- Users can give positive/negative feedback with minimal friction (1 click)
- Feedback is captured and accessible for review (not lost to the void)
- Widget does not degrade page load performance
- Consistent with cosalette brand and docs site design
- Works on mobile

Improve commands() shutdown responsiveness for long timeouts
description:
When ctx.commands(timeout=N) is used with large timeout values (e.g. 60s), the asyncio.wait_for() call blocks for up to N seconds before re-checking shutdown_requested. This means graceful shutdown latency equals the timeout value in the worst case.

## Current behaviour

The commands() iterator uses asyncio.wait_for(queue.get(), timeout=poll) where poll equals the user-supplied timeout. During the wait, the shutdown event is not monitored — the loop only checks shutdown_requested after wait_for completes or times out.

## Proposed fix

Wait concurrently on _command_queue.get() and _shutdown_event.wait() using asyncio.wait(return_when=FIRST_COMPLETED), matching the pattern already used by ctx.sleep(). This keeps shutdown responsive (≤1s latency) regardless of the configured timeout value, while preserving the public timeout semantics (yield None after N seconds of no commands).

Copilot reviewer suggested a deadline-based short-poll slicing approach as an alternative — see PR #129 inline comment on _context.py line 280 for the full suggested implementation. Either approach works; the asyncio.wait dual-task pattern is simpler and consistent with ctx.sleep().

## Files to modify

- packages/src/cosalette/_context.py — commands() inner _iter() generator
- packages/tests/unit/test_context.py — add test with long timeout + early shutdown

## Acceptance criteria

1. Shutdown latency ≤1s regardless of timeout value
2. Timeout semantics unchanged — yield None after N seconds of no commands
3. Existing tests continue to pass
